explanation: `git --version` is the standard verification command. If it fails, Git is either not installed or not in your system PATH.
tip: On macOS, running `git --version` before installing Git will prompt you to install Xcode Command Line Tools.

explanation: `--global` is the flag you will use most. It sets your name for all repos. `--local` overrides per repo, `--system` applies to all users on the machine.
tip: Order of priority: local overrides global, global overrides system.

explanation: The `.gitconfig` file in your home directory is a plain text file. You can open and edit it directly in any text editor.
tip: Run `cat ~/.gitconfig` in your terminal to see the raw file contents.

explanation: `git config --list` is your verification command. Add `--show-origin` to see which file each setting comes from.
tip: Look for `user.name=` and `user.email=` in the output to confirm your identity is set.

explanation: GitHub's contribution graph, blame view, and author attribution all rely on email matching. Always use the same email.
tip: If your email is private, GitHub provides a no-reply email like `12345678+username@users.noreply.github.com`.

explanation: Git Bash gives you a full bash environment on Windows. It is bundled with Git for Windows — no separate install needed.
tip: Right-click in any folder and choose 'Git Bash Here' to open Git Bash in that location.

explanation: `--local` is useful when you work with multiple GitHub accounts or when a project needs different settings than your global defaults.
tip: Example: Work project uses work email (--local), personal projects use personal email (--global).

explanation: The `--wait` flag is crucial. Without it, Git continues immediately after opening VS Code, before you have finished writing the commit message.
tip: For nano: `git config --global core.editor nano`. For Vim: `git config --global core.editor vim`.

explanation: Any valid version number means Git is installed and working. If you get 'command not found', Git is not in your PATH.
tip: Git 2.x has been standard since 2014. You rarely need to worry about version compatibility.

explanation: GitHub renamed the default branch from 'master' to 'main' in 2020. Setting this locally ensures your repos match GitHub's default.
tip: Run this once after installing Git: `git config --global init.defaultBranch main`
